# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Effect of training hours on productivity

**Conclusion: positive effect.** Preferred estimate: +0.841 thousand USD of 2023 value added per employee for each 1-unit increase in training_hours. SE 0.241 (HC1 robust), p = 0.0005, 95% CI about [0.37, 1.31]. N = 2000.

training_hours is standardized (mean 0). I assume 1 unit is about 1 SD, but the codebook does not say. The effect is small: roughly 0.07 SD of productivity_2023 (SD 11.4).

**Preferred specification:** OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours plus all pre-period covariates, with HC1 SEs. The covariates are log_employees_2020, firm_age_2020, productivity_2020, region, listed, sector, export_share_2020, foreign_owned, family_owned, rd_intensity_2020, union_share_2020 and credit_score_2020.

Training is not randomized. The estimate is causal only if the pre-period controls remove all confounding. Unobserved confounders could still bias it. The raw association (2.37) is about three times the adjusted one, so confounding by pre-period characteristics was substantial. Some may remain.

**Excluded control:** mgmt_rating_2023 was measured in 2023, after training. It is a possible mediator or collider. Controlling for it turns the estimate sharply negative (-2.09), which is the pattern that bad-control bias would produce. I do not treat that specification as valid.

## All specifications estimated (7; all OLS with HC1 SEs, N = 2000)
| # | Specification | Coef on training_hours | SE | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Raw bivariate | 2.373 | 0.239 | 2.7e-23 |
| 2 | + log_employees, firm_age, productivity_2020 | 0.798 | 0.241 | 0.0009 |
| 3 | **Full pre-period controls (preferred)** | **0.841** | **0.241** | **0.0005** |
| 4 | Full pre-period controls + mgmt_rating_2023 (bad control, rejected) | -2.089 | 0.234 | 3.9e-19 |
| 5 | log(productivity_2023), full pre-period controls | 0.0088 (about 0.9%) | 0.0024 | 0.0003 |
| 6 | Full pre-period controls + quadratic term | linear 0.841 (quadratic 0.004, p = 0.98, so no curvature) | 0.242 | 0.0005 |
| 7 | Full pre-period controls without productivity_2020 | 0.905 | 0.240 | 0.0002 |

Every specification that uses only pre-treatment controls (2, 3, 5, 6, 7) gives a positive, significant effect of similar size. Only the raw estimate (1) is larger, and only the post-treatment control (4) reverses the sign.

import pandas as pd, numpy as np, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
d=pd.read_csv('data.csv')
print(d.describe().T)
print(d.isna().sum().sum())
pre="log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020+C(region)+listed+C(sector)+export_share_2020+foreign_owned+family_owned+rd_intensity_2020+union_share_2020+credit_score_2020"
S={'raw':'productivity_2023~training_hours',
'core':'productivity_2023~training_hours+log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020',
'full_pre':'productivity_2023~training_hours+'+pre,
'full_pre+mgmt':'productivity_2023~training_hours+mgmt_rating_2023+'+pre,
'logY_full_pre':'np.log(productivity_2023)~training_hours+'+pre,
'quad_full_pre':'productivity_2023~training_hours+I(training_hours**2)+'+pre,
'no_lagY':'productivity_2023~training_hours+'+pre.replace('+productivity_2020',''),
}
for k,f in S.items():
    m=smf.ols(f,d).fit(cov_type='HC1')
    print(k,m.params['training_hours'],m.bse['training_hours'],m.pvalues['training_hours'],m.nobs)
    if k=='quad_full_pre': print(m.params['I(training_hours ** 2)'],m.pvalues['I(training_hours ** 2)'])
m=smf.ols('productivity_2023~training_hours+'+pre,d).fit(cov_type='HC1');print(m.summary())
print(d.productivity_2023.describe())

content.text:
I approved the report and wrote `verdict.json`. The conclusion of a small positive effect holds up.

- **Replication:** I re-ran the preferred model and got the reported +0.841 (SE 0.241, p ≈ 0.0005, N = 2000).
- **Controls:** The model adjusts only for pre-period covariates. It correctly leaves out `mgmt_rating_2023`, which was measured after training and flips the sign when included.
- **Robustness:** The report lists all 7 specifications it estimated. The positive effect holds in every one that uses only pre-treatment controls.
- **Causal caveat:** The report states that training was not randomized and that unobserved confounding could remain. That is the main limit on a causal reading.
- **Sector split (not in the report):** By sector, the estimate is about 1.37 for manufacturing and 0.30 for services. This doesn't change the overall conclusion, but the effect looks stronger in manufacturing.

I did not check whether the one-unit scale of `training_hours` is one standard deviation. The report flags that itself, because the codebook doesn't say.
